title: Analytics Engineering and Data Governance
description: How raw data becomes trusted analysis: dimensional models, transformation layers, tests and metrics, then lineage, quality, privacy and the roles that govern all of it.
audience: A capable adult who can write SQL joins and aggregates (sql-from-rows-to-reports) and has seen a data pipeline (data-engineering helps but is not required). No previous modelling or governance knowledge assumed. Tools such as dbt are named only as examples.
outcomes: You'll be able to declare a grain and design a star schema around it.
You'll be able to keep history in dimensions and avoid fan-out in joins.
You'll be able to place logic in layers, write data tests and define metrics once.
You'll be able to trace lineage, measure quality and read a contract and a service level.
You'll be able to classify and protect personal data and explain what governance has to do in practice.

modules.summary: Grain, facts and dimensions, slowly changing history and the trade-offs between model shapes.

modules.title: Transformation layers

lessons.title: From questions to grain
lessons.objective: Turn a business question into a business process and a declared grain, and recognise a fact table whose grain is mixed.

concepts.title: Business process
concepts.summary: A measurable activity the business performs, such as taking an order or shipping a parcel, produces the events a model records.

concepts.title: Grain
concepts.summary: The grain states exactly what one row of a fact table represents, such as one order line, and every column must be true at that grain.

concepts.title: Four design steps
concepts.summary: Dimensional design chooses the business process, declares the grain, identifies the dimensions and identifies the facts, in that order.

concepts.title: Star schema
concepts.summary: A fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive context, joined by keys.

misconceptions: Learners start from the available columns. The grain comes from the question and the process, and columns follow.
Learners put order totals on an order-line table. The total is true at order grain, so summing it over lines repeats it.
Learners think more detail is always better. Grain must be fine enough for the questions but no finer than the data supports.
sequence: Start with 'what share of orders ship late?' and name the process and grain.
Declare order line as the grain and list what is true at that grain: quantity, unit price, line amount.
Show an order_total column on the line table and total it.
Draw the star: orders fact with date, customer and product dimensions.
examples: Grain: one row per order line. Quantity 2 and line amount 40.00 are true at that grain; the order's shipping fee of 5.00 is not, and storing it on both of two lines would double it to 10.00 when summed.
Orders of 100, 200 and 300 with 2, 1 and 3 lines: summing an order_total repeated on each line gives 100x2 + 200x1 + 300x3 = 1,300 instead of 600.
A star for retail sales has a sales fact (grain: one row per product per receipt line) and dimensions date, store, product and customer.

figures.shows: A star schema with the fact table in the centre and four dimensions around it; a banner shows the declared grain in words. Views: star, grain sentence, a mixed-grain mistake highlighted.
figures.learnerAction: Change the grain statement and see which columns are no longer true at that grain.

figures.shows: A small order-lines table with an order_total column repeated, using different orders from the question, and a SUM row.
figures.learnerAction: Sum the column and compare it with the total of the distinct orders.

questionPlan.sample: Which is a well-formed grain statement for a sales fact table?
questionPlan.answer: One row per product on each receipt line
choices: One row per product on each receipt line

questionPlan.sample: Orders of 100, 200 and 300 have 2, 1 and 3 order lines. An order_total column is copied onto each line. What does SUM(order_total) over the line table return?
'How long does it take to ship an order after payment?' Which business process does the model record? Answer in two words.

lessons.title: Facts and dimensions
lessons.objective: Classify measures as additive, semi-additive or non-additive, choose between transaction, periodic snapshot and accumulating snapshot facts, and explain surrogate keys.

concepts.title: Additivity
concepts.summary: Additive measures can be summed across every dimension, semi-additive ones across all but time, and non-additive ones such as ratios not at all.

concepts.title: Fact table types
concepts.summary: A transaction fact records events, a periodic snapshot records state at regular intervals, and an accumulating snapshot tracks one row through a process with several dates.

concepts.title: Surrogate key
concepts.summary: A meaningless integer key owned by the warehouse, which survives changes in source keys and allows history.

concepts.title: Degenerate dimension
concepts.summary: An identifier such as an order number kept on the fact table because it has no attributes of its own.

misconceptions: Learners sum account balances over days. A balance is a state at a moment, and the total of three days' balances means nothing.
Learners average a ratio column. Ratios must be rebuilt from their additive parts.
Learners use the source's business key as the join key. It can change, repeat across systems or lose history.
sequence: An account with balances 100, 120 and 90 on three days.
Which aggregation works for each of quantity sold, unit price, margin percent and balance.
Three fact types for one retail business: sales lines, daily stock levels, and order-to-delivery progress.
Why dim_customer has customer_key as well as customer_id.
examples: Balances of 100, 120 and 90 on Monday to Wednesday sum to 310, which is meaningless; the end-of-period balance is 90 and the average is 103.33.
Quantity and revenue are additive; unit price and margin percent are non-additive; account balance and stock level are semi-additive (sum across accounts, not across days).
A periodic snapshot of stock has one row per product per day; an accumulating snapshot of orders has one row per order with dates for ordered, paid, shipped and delivered.

figures.shows: A fact table of daily account balances for different accounts and values from the questions, with aggregation buttons (sum, average, last) and a sum-across-accounts row.
figures.learnerAction: Try each aggregation across time and across accounts.

figures.shows: Four business processes with a choice of fact table type.
figures.learnerAction: Match process to fact type.

questionPlan.sample: Which measure is semi-additive?
An account's balance was 100 on Monday, 120 on Tuesday and 90 on Wednesday. What is its balance for the period, taking the end-of-period value?
Which fact table type has one row per order, updated as the order moves through paid, shipped and delivered?

lessons.title: History in dimensions
lessons.objective: Choose between overwriting and versioning a dimension attribute, and join a fact to the dimension row that was true on the transaction date.

concepts.title: Slowly changing dimension
concepts.summary: An attribute of a dimension, such as a customer's city, changes occasionally, and the model must decide whether the past should show the old or the new value.

concepts.title: Type 1 and Type 2
concepts.summary: Type 1 overwrites the value and loses history, while Type 2 adds a new row with validity dates so history is kept.

concepts.title: As-of join
concepts.summary: A fact joins the dimension row whose validity range contains the fact's date.

concepts.title: Conformed dimensions
concepts.summary: A dimension shared by several fact tables with identical keys and meaning, so their results can be combined.

misconceptions: Learners overwrite attributes to keep the model simple, then find last year's revenue moves to the customer's new city.
Learners join facts to the current dimension row only. That puts every past sale in the present attribute.
Learners use closed end dates and overlapping ranges, which makes a fact match two rows.
sequence: Customer C1 moved from Leeds to York on 2026-03-01 and has three sales.
Total by city under Type 1 and under Type 2.
Validity ranges: valid_from inclusive, valid_to exclusive, with 9999-12-31 for the current row.
Other SCD types in one line each: 0 keeps the original, 3 adds a previous-value column, 6 combines 1, 2 and 3.
examples: As-of join by city: Leeds 100 (50+30 from C1 and 20 from C2), York 70.
Joining only to current rows (Type 1 behaviour): Leeds 20, York 150.

figures.shows: The dim_customer and sales tables for a different example (a salesperson who changes region), with editable join conditions and live result.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between a current-row join and an as-of join and read the totals.

figures.shows: A date axis with validity bars for each version of a dimension row and sale dots that attach to the bar they fall in.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a sale across the change date.

questionPlan.sample: Setup: CREATE TABLE dim_customer(sk INT, cust_id TEXT, city TEXT, valid_from TEXT, valid_to TEXT); INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (1,'C1','Leeds','2025-01-01','2026-03-01'),(2,'C1','York','2026-03-01','9999-12-31'),(3,'C2','Leeds','2025-01-01','9999-12-31'); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT,cust_id TEXT,sale_date TEXT,amount INT); INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'C1','2026-01-15',50),(2,'C1','2026-02-20',30),(3,'C1','2026-04-02',70),(4,'C2','2026-04-03',20); Join sales to dim_customer on cust_id with sale_date >= valid_from AND sale_date < valid_to. What is the York total?
With the same tables, join only to the current rows (valid_to = '9999-12-31'). What is the York total?
Finance must report each past sale under the sales region the account manager belonged to at the time. Which approach?
questionPlan.answer: Type 2: keep a row per version with validity dates
choices: Type 2: keep a row per version with validity dates
Store the region only in the report

lessons.title: Choosing a model shape
lessons.objective: Choose between a star schema, a normalised model, one wide table and a data vault for a given need, and detect a join fan-out before it inflates a total.

concepts.title: Normalised and dimensional
concepts.summary: A normalised model avoids redundancy for updating, a dimensional model repeats descriptions to make reading simple and fast.

concepts.title: One big table
concepts.summary: A denormalised wide table is easy to query for one purpose but repeats data and hides grain.

concepts.title: Data vault
concepts.summary: A model of hubs (keys), links (relationships) and satellites (history) built for auditable integration from many sources, usually with marts built on top.

concepts.title: Join fan-out
concepts.summary: Joining a one-to-many relationship repeats the parent row once per child, so a parent measure summed after the join is inflated.

misconceptions: Learners think one shape suits every layer. Integration, history and reporting have different needs.
Learners join orders to items and sum the order total. Each order repeats once per item.
Learners think a bigger model is a better model. Each added table adds joins and ways to be wrong.
sequence: Compare three shapes of the same retail data by what is easy and what is hard.
Join 3 orders to 6 items and sum order totals.
Fix it by aggregating items first or summing at the right grain.
Place data vault as an integration layer feeding stars.
examples: Orders of 100, 200 and 300 joined to items (2, 1 and 3 lines) give SUM(o.total) = 1,300 after the join, but 600 from the orders table alone.
Aggregating items to one row per order before the join keeps the sum at 600.
A star is the best default for reporting, a data vault for many-source integration with audit needs, and a wide table as a final convenience mart.

figures.shows: Two tables, invoices and invoice lines (different from the questions), with a join that can be toggled between raw and pre-aggregated, and totals shown for each.
figures.learnerAction: Run both joins and compare totals.

figures.shows: Four scenarios (ad hoc dashboard, many-source audit, transactional app, data science feature table) with a choice of shape.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the shape for each.

questionPlan.sample: Setup: CREATE TABLE o(id INT, total INT); INSERT INTO o VALUES (1,100),(2,200),(3,300); CREATE TABLE i(oid INT, sku TEXT); INSERT INTO i VALUES (1,'a'),(1,'b'),(2,'c'),(3,'a'),(3,'b'),(3,'c'); What does SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM o JOIN i ON i.oid = o.id return?
With the same tables, what does SELECT SUM(total) FROM o return?
Which shape fits integrating ten source systems with full audit history before building reports?

lessons.title: Layers of models
lessons.objective: Place a transformation in a staging, intermediate or mart layer, choose a materialisation, and read a model graph.

concepts.title: Staging
concepts.summary: Staging models mirror one source table each, renaming columns, fixing types and changing nothing else.

concepts.title: Intermediate and marts
concepts.summary: Intermediate models join and reshape, and marts present business entities and measures for use.

concepts.title: Materialisation
concepts.summary: A model can be built as a view, a table, an incremental table or inlined as ephemeral, trading build time against query time and freshness.

concepts.title: Model graph
concepts.summary: Models refer to each other by reference rather than table name, so the tool builds a graph and runs models in dependency order.

misconceptions: Learners put business logic in staging. Staging must stay boring so every downstream model sees the same cleaned source.
Learners materialise everything as tables. Views cost nothing to build and tables cost nothing to read; each has its place.
Learners hard-code table names. References let the tool order the build and trace lineage.
sequence: Show raw orders to stg_orders, int_orders_joined, fct_orders.
Choose a materialisation for a 2 billion row event model refreshed hourly.
Read a graph of eight models and find what runs first.
Reference by ref('stg_orders') rather than a schema.table string.
examples: stg_orders renames orderid to order_id and casts amount to a decimal; int_orders_joined joins it to customers; fct_orders is the mart.
A multi-billion-row append-mostly event model is a good incremental table; a small lookup is a view.
In dbt, ref('stg_orders') is how one model refers to another, and the tool builds the dependency graph from those calls (an example, not a requirement).

figures.shows: A model graph from sources through staging, intermediate and mart models, with a legend for materialisation and a build-order numbering. Views: layers, materialisation, build order.
figures.learnerAction: Click a model to highlight what it needs and what needs it.

figures.shows: Five transformations (rename a column, join orders to customers, daily revenue by region, cast a date, a one-off helper) with a layer choice.
figures.learnerAction: Place each in a layer.

questionPlan.sample: Where should casting amount from text to a decimal and renaming orderid to order_id happen?
questionPlan.answer: In the staging model for that source
choices: In the staging model for that source

questionPlan.sample: A model with several billion rows grows by appending new events each hour. Which materialisation suits it?
In dbt, which function does one model use to refer to another so the tool can order the build? Give the function name.

lessons.title: Incremental builds
lessons.objective: Predict which rows an incremental model picks up and which it misses, and choose a lookback or snapshot to close the gap.

concepts.title: Incremental filter
concepts.summary: An incremental run selects only rows newer than the maximum timestamp already in the target and merges them by key.

concepts.title: Lookback window
concepts.summary: Re-reading a recent window each run catches late-arriving rows, and a unique key keeps the re-read from duplicating.

concepts.title: Full refresh
concepts.summary: Rebuilding the whole model from scratch repairs logic changes and missed rows at the cost of a long build.

concepts.title: Snapshots
concepts.summary: A snapshot records how a mutable source row changes over time, adding validity dates, so history exists when the source overwrites it.

misconceptions: Learners think an incremental model always matches a full refresh. It matches only if late rows and changed logic are handled.
Learners think a unique key alone catches late rows. The filter must read them first.
Learners forget that a changed model definition does not rewrite old rows. A full refresh is needed.
sequence: A target with ids 1 to 3 and a source with ids 1 to 5, updated on different days.
Run the max(updated_at) filter and list the ids it reads.
Show the missed late row, then a 3-day lookback.
Snapshots: use a timestamp strategy to capture a row's changes.
examples: Target max updated_at is 2026-05-03. Source rows: id 1 (05-01), id 2 changed to v=25 (05-04), id 3 (05-03), id 4 new (05-04), id 5 late (05-02). The filter updated_at > 2026-05-03 reads ids 2 and 4.
After the merge the target holds ids 1, 2 (v=25), 3 and 4: four rows; id 5 is missed because its timestamp is older than the max.
A lookback of 3 days (updated_at > max - 3 days) re-reads ids 3 and 5, and the unique key avoids duplicates.

figures.shows: A target table, a source table and a run button for the incremental filter, with a lookback slider, using a different table (invoices).
figures.learnerAction: Run the filter and change the lookback.

figures.shows: A time axis with source commits and the max timestamp marker, plus the late row falling behind it.
figures.learnerAction: Move the marker and see which rows read.

questionPlan.sample: Setup: CREATE TABLE tgt(id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT, updated_at TEXT); INSERT INTO tgt VALUES (1,10,'2026-05-01'),(2,20,'2026-05-02'),(3,30,'2026-05-03'); CREATE TABLE src(id INT, v INT, updated_at TEXT); INSERT INTO src VALUES (1,10,'2026-05-01'),(2,25,'2026-05-04'),(3,30,'2026-05-03'),(4,40,'2026-05-04'),(5,50,'2026-05-02'); Merge rows with updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM tgt) into tgt by id. How many rows does tgt hold afterwards?
Which source id is never loaded by that filter? Give the id.
Which change makes the incremental model pick up late-arriving rows?
questionPlan.answer: Re-read a recent window and merge on the unique key
choices: Delete the target and never rebuild
Re-read a recent window and merge on the unique key
Use a strict greater-than on the max timestamp

lessons.title: Testing data
lessons.objective: Write a test as a query that returns failing rows, read the result of the four standard tests, and choose where in the graph a test belongs.

concepts.title: Tests return failing rows
concepts.summary: A data test is a query written so that it returns the rows that break the assertion, and it passes when it returns none.

concepts.title: The standard four
concepts.summary: unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships cover most structural assumptions about a column.

concepts.title: Where to test
concepts.summary: Test sources for what you receive, staging for keys, and marts for business rules, because a failure is cheapest to explain closest to its cause.

concepts.title: Unit tests and data tests
concepts.summary: A data test checks real data after a build, while a unit test checks the transformation logic against small fixed inputs.

misconceptions: Learners write tests that return a count of passes. A test must return the failing rows so the cause can be seen.
Learners expect unique to count NULLs as duplicates. A not_null test handles those.
Learners test only the final mart. By then the cause is hours away.
sequence: customers with email values including a repeat and two NULLs, and orders with customer ids.
unique returns the repeated value; not_null returns the NULL rows.
relationships returns orders whose customer id has no match, ignoring NULL ids.
accepted_values returns orders with a status not on the list.
examples: customers emails: a@x.com, NULL, a@x.com, d@x.com, NULL. A unique test returns 1 failing value (a@x.com, appearing twice) and a not_null test returns 2 rows.
orders with customer_ids 1, 2, 9, 3, NULL, 4, 12: a relationships test against customers 1 to 5 returns orders with customer ids 9 and 12.
orders with statuses paid, paid, shipped, refunded, paid, void, paid: accepted_values for (paid, shipped, refunded) returns the one 'void' order.

figures.shows: Two tables with failing-rows queries for each standard test and a pass/fail strip, using a different example (employees and departments).
figures.learnerAction: Run each test and read the failing rows.

figures.shows: A graph of models with tests as flags, and the learner chooses the best layer for four tests.
figures.learnerAction: Place each test.

questionPlan.sample: Setup: CREATE TABLE customers(id INT, email TEXT); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,NULL),(3,'a@x.com'),(4,'d@x.com'),(5,NULL); CREATE TABLE orders(id INT, customer_id INT, status TEXT); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,'paid'),(11,2,'paid'),(12,9,'shipped'),(13,3,'refunded'),(14,NULL,'paid'),(15,4,'void'),(16,12,'paid'); Write the relationships test: orders whose non-null customer_id has no matching customers.id. Which order ids are returned, in ascending order?
With the same customers table, how many rows does a not_null test on email return?
With the same orders table, which order id fails an accepted_values test for status in ('paid','shipped','refunded')?

lessons.title: Semantic layers and metrics
lessons.objective: Define a metric once from additive parts, explain why a ratio of sums differs from an average of ratios, and avoid double counting distinct measures across groups.

concepts.title: Metric
concepts.summary: A named calculation, such as revenue or average order value, with an agreed definition, grain and filters.

concepts.title: Semantic layer
concepts.summary: A layer that defines metrics and dimensions once, so every dashboard and query returns the same number.

concepts.title: Metric types
concepts.summary: Simple metrics aggregate a measure, ratio metrics divide two metrics, cumulative metrics accumulate over time and derived metrics combine metrics.

concepts.title: Non-additive metrics
concepts.summary: Distinct counts and ratios cannot be added across groups, and must be recomputed at the requested grain.

misconceptions: Learners average per-region averages. The overall average is a ratio of totals.
Learners add distinct customer counts across regions. A customer in two regions is counted twice.
Learners redefine revenue in each dashboard. Two numbers for one name destroy trust.
sequence: Two regions: A has revenue 100 and 10 orders; B has revenue 900 and 30 orders.
Average of average order values versus total revenue over total orders.
Customers in A: 1, 2, 3. Customers in B: 3, 4.
Define 'revenue' once, with its filters, and reuse it.
examples: Average order value: region A 100/10 = 10, region B 900/30 = 30. The average of the two is 20, but the overall value is (100+900)/(10+30) = 25.
Distinct customers: A has {1,2,3}, B has {3,4}; the sum of counts is 5, the distinct count over both is 4.
A ratio metric stores numerator and denominator metrics, and the tool divides after aggregating.

figures.shows: Two other regions (different numbers from the questions) with revenue, orders and AOV, and buttons for 'average the AOVs' and 'total over total'.
figures.learnerAction: Try both and compare with a hidden reference.

figures.shows: Two overlapping circles for customers in two other regions (different ids from the questions) with counts and the distinct union.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between sum of counts and distinct count.

questionPlan.sample: Region A has revenue 100 from 10 orders and region B has revenue 900 from 30 orders. What is the overall average order value?
Region A's customers are 1, 2 and 3, and region B's are 3 and 4. How many distinct customers are there overall?
Two dashboards show different 'revenue' for the same month. What fixes it at the cause?
questionPlan.answer: Define revenue once in a shared metric layer and reuse it
choices: Tell users which dashboard to trust
Define revenue once in a shared metric layer and reuse it

lessons.title: Lineage
lessons.objective: Read a lineage graph to list everything upstream or downstream of a node, and say what an impact analysis and a column-level lineage add.

concepts.title: Lineage
concepts.summary: A record of which datasets and jobs produced which other datasets, so data can be traced back to sources and forward to uses.

concepts.title: Upstream and downstream
concepts.summary: Upstream nodes feed a dataset, and downstream nodes consume it, directly or through other nodes.

concepts.title: Impact analysis
concepts.summary: Walking downstream from a changing node lists the models, reports and owners that a change can break.

concepts.title: Lineage events
concepts.summary: Jobs can emit run events naming their input and output datasets, and a lineage store assembles them into a graph.

misconceptions: Learners think lineage is a drawing. It is captured from runs, so it stays true when jobs change.
Learners count only direct consumers. An impact reaches everything downstream, however many hops.
Learners think table-level lineage is enough. A broken column needs column-level lineage to see which outputs really use it.
sequence: Draw sources s1 and s2 into stg1 and stg2, then int1, mart1, mart2 and dashboards d1 and d2.
List everything downstream of stg1 and upstream of d2.
Impact: if s2 changes shape, which dashboards are affected?
Show a run event with a job, a run, and input and output datasets.
examples: Edges: s1 to stg1; s2 to stg2; stg1 and stg2 to int1; int1 to mart1; stg2 to mart2; mart1 to d1 and d2; mart2 to d2.
Downstream of stg1: int1, mart1, d1, d2 (4 nodes). Upstream of d2: mart1, mart2, int1, stg1, stg2, s1, s2 (7 nodes).
If s2 changes, the affected dashboards are d1 and d2 (2): d1 through stg2, int1, mart1; d2 through mart1 and mart2.

figures.shows: A different lineage graph from the one in the questions, with selectable nodes: choosing one highlights upstream in one colour and downstream in another and shows counts. Views: table-level, column-level for one mart.
figures.learnerAction: Click nodes and read the highlighted sets.

figures.shows: A list of run events (start, complete) with job and dataset names that build the graph step by step.
figures.learnerAction: Step through the events and watch edges appear.

questionPlan.sample: Edges: s1 to stg1; s2 to stg2; stg1 and stg2 to int1; int1 to mart1; stg2 to mart2; mart1 to d1 and d2; mart2 to d2. How many nodes are downstream of stg1?
In the same graph, how many nodes are upstream of d2?
In the same graph, source s2 changes shape. How many dashboards (d1, d2) can be affected?

lessons.title: Measuring quality
lessons.objective: Compute completeness, uniqueness and freshness, and use a z-score against recent history to flag an abnormal volume.

concepts.title: Quality dimensions
concepts.summary: Completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency and timeliness name different ways data can be wrong.

concepts.title: Quality as a rate
concepts.summary: Each dimension becomes a rate, such as non-null rows over all rows, compared with a threshold agreed with the data's users.

concepts.title: Volume anomalies
concepts.summary: A z-score, the distance from the recent mean in standard deviations, flags a day whose row count is unusual.

concepts.title: Freshness target
concepts.summary: Timeliness is measured as age against a target, and a breach is the amount by which the age exceeds it.

misconceptions: Learners treat quality as a pass or fail. Quality is a rate with a threshold that matches a use.
Learners test accuracy with rules only. Accuracy needs an external reference; rules catch validity and consistency.
Learners set a fixed row-count limit. Volumes drift and have seasons, so compare with recent history.
sequence: 940 non-null emails in 1,000 rows.
980 distinct ids in 1,000 rows.
Daily row counts in thousands: 95, 105, 95, 105, then 85 today.
A table last updated at 03:00, checked at 09:00 against a 4-hour target.
examples: Completeness: 940 / 1,000 = 94%. Uniqueness: 980 distinct of 1,000 rows = 98%.
History 95, 105, 95, 105 has mean 100 and population standard deviation 5; a count of 85 has z = (85-100)/5 = -3.0.
A table updated at 03:00 and checked at 09:00 is 6 hours old; against a 4-hour target it breaches by 2 hours.

figures.shows: A bar chart of a different week of daily row counts (not the history in the questions) with mean and plus or minus 3 standard deviation lines and a movable 'today' bar.
figures.learnerAction: Drag today's count and read its z-score.

figures.shows: A quality scorecard with completeness, uniqueness and freshness for several columns and target colours.
figures.learnerAction: Set thresholds and see which columns fail.

questionPlan.sample: 940 of 1,000 rows have a non-null email. What is the completeness, in percent?
Daily row counts (thousands) were 95, 105, 95 and 105. Using the population standard deviation, what is the z-score of today's count of 85?
A table was last updated at 03:00 and it is 09:00. Its freshness target is 4 hours. By how many hours is it in breach?

lessons.title: Contracts, ownership and service levels
lessons.objective: Classify a schema change as breaking or compatible, work out an error budget from a service-level objective, and say who owns a failing dataset.

concepts.title: Data contract
concepts.summary: An agreement between a producer and its consumers on schema, meaning, quality and timeliness of a dataset, checked automatically.

concepts.title: Breaking change
concepts.summary: Removing, renaming or retyping a field, or changing its meaning, breaks consumers, while adding an optional field does not.

concepts.title: Service-level objective
concepts.summary: A target for a measurable indicator, such as 99% of days with data ready by 07:00, over a set period.

concepts.title: Error budget
concepts.summary: The allowed failure implied by the objective, such as 1% of a 30-day month, which is 7.2 hours.

misconceptions: Learners think a contract is a document. It is a machine-checked agreement, or it will drift.
Learners think a new column cannot break anyone. A consumer that selects every column or enforces a fixed schema can break.
Learners assign ownership to the pipeline team for everything. The producing domain owns the meaning; the platform owns the tooling.
sequence: List five changes and mark each breaking or compatible.
Turn 99% over 30 days into hours.
A failed freshness check at 07:00: who is paged, who is told.
A contract file with schema, quality and SLO sections.
examples: Compatible: adding an optional column. Breaking: removing a column, renaming a column, changing a type from integer to string, changing 'amount' from gross to net.
99% over 30 days (720 hours) allows 1% = 7.2 hours of failure; 99.5% allows 3.6 hours.
The Open Data Contract Standard describes schema, quality and service-level sections in one YAML document (an example, not a requirement).

figures.shows: A change list with columns for the change, who is affected and a breaking/compatible mark hidden until chosen.
figures.learnerAction: Classify each change.

figures.shows: A month calendar with failed days shaded against an error budget bar that drains.
figures.learnerAction: Click days to fail and watch the budget.

choices: Renaming the column order_total to total

lessons.title: Classifying and protecting data
lessons.objective: Classify data by sensitivity, tell hashing and pseudonymisation from anonymisation, and compute k for a table to judge re-identification risk.

concepts.title: Classification
concepts.summary: Data is labelled by sensitivity, such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, and the label drives who can see it and how it is stored.

concepts.title: Personal data
concepts.summary: Any information relating to an identifiable person, including indirect identifiers such as a postcode and age together.

concepts.title: Pseudonymisation and anonymisation
concepts.summary: Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers but can be reversed or guessed and remains personal data, while true anonymisation cannot be linked back to a person.

concepts.title: k-anonymity
concepts.summary: A table has k-anonymity when every combination of quasi-identifiers appears at least k times, so no row is unique among its group.

misconceptions: Learners think hashing an email makes it anonymous. An unsalted hash of a guessable value can be matched by hashing candidates.
Learners remove names and call the data anonymous. Age, postcode and sex together can identify people.
Learners protect only the columns marked PII. Combinations of ordinary columns can re-identify.
sequence: Classify columns of a customer table by sensitivity.
Hash an email: why a list of known emails reverses it.
Count how many rows share each (age band, postcode prefix, sex).
Generalise rows until every group has at least 3.
examples: Table of 8 rows with (age band, postcode prefix, sex): (30-39, LS1, F) x3, (40-49, LS2, M) x3, (20-29, LS1, M) x1, (30-39, LS1, M) x1. Group sizes are 3, 3, 1, 1, so k = 1.
To reach k = 3 the two rows in single-row groups must be generalised or removed.
An unsalted SHA-256 hash of a known email matches the hash of the same email computed by anyone, so it is pseudonymous at best.

figures.shows: A table of other rows (not the question's rows) with quasi-identifier columns, coloured by group size, and a generalise button that widens an age band.
figures.learnerAction: Generalise until every group is at least 3.

figures.shows: Six columns of a customer table with a choice of sensitivity label.
figures.learnerAction: Label each column.

questionPlan.sample: Rows (age band, postcode prefix, sex): (30-39, LS1, F) x3; (40-49, LS2, M) x3; (20-29, LS1, M) x1; (30-39, LS1, M) x1. What is the k of this table?
For the same table, how many rows lie in groups smaller than 3 and so block k = 3?
Replacing an email with an unsalted hash of the email is an example of which technique, which still leaves personal data? Give the one word.

lessons.title: Privacy law in practice
lessons.objective: Explain the main GDPR principles, lawful bases and data subject rights, and show how an erasure request works in a table format with immutable files.

concepts.title: Principles
concepts.summary: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, for specified purposes, minimally, accurately, for no longer than needed, and securely, with the controller accountable.

concepts.title: Lawful bases
concepts.summary: There are six lawful bases for processing: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.

concepts.title: Data subject rights
concepts.summary: People may access their data, correct it, have it erased in some cases, restrict or object to processing, and receive it in a portable format.

concepts.title: Erasure in immutable storage
concepts.summary: Deleting a row in a table format writes a new version, and the old files remain on storage until they are vacuumed.

misconceptions: Learners think consent is always required. It is one of six lawful bases, and often not the right one.
Learners think a SQL DELETE ends the obligation. In a versioned table the old files still hold the data until vacuum, and backups still hold it too.
Learners treat privacy as a legal-team matter. Retention, minimisation and erasure are engineering designs.
sequence: Walk through the seven principles in plain words.
Pick lawful bases for three processing activities.
Map access, rectification, erasure and portability to engineering tasks.
Erase one customer from a Delta table: delete, then vacuum after retention, then backups.
The 72-hour breach notification rule.
examples: Under GDPR a controller must notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it (Article 33).
Administrative fines can reach 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 83(5)); for a company with 1 billion euros turnover that is 40 million euros.
A DELETE in Delta writes a new version; with a vacuum retention of 7 days the old files with the person's data are removed only after the retention has passed and the vacuum runs.

figures.shows: A timeline of an erasure request: request, delete commit, retention window, vacuum, backup expiry, with the data's remaining copies shown at each point.
figures.learnerAction: Step forward in time and see where the data still exists.

figures.shows: Five processing activities with candidate lawful bases.
figures.learnerAction: Choose a lawful basis for each.

questionPlan.answer: After the old versions are vacuumed past the retention period
choices: After the old versions are vacuumed past the retention period

lessons.title: Governance in practice
lessons.objective: Assign owner, steward and custodian roles, describe what a catalogue and glossary record, and sketch a governance process that people will actually follow.

concepts.title: Governance roles
concepts.summary: The owner is accountable for a dataset, the steward maintains its definitions and quality, and the custodian runs the platform that stores it.

concepts.title: Catalogue and glossary
concepts.summary: A catalogue records technical, business and operational metadata for datasets, and a glossary fixes the meaning of business terms.

concepts.title: From policy to control
concepts.summary: A policy becomes a rule the platform enforces, such as a masking rule on a classified column or a retention job, rather than a document to remember.

concepts.title: Certified datasets
concepts.summary: A dataset marked as reviewed, owned and monitored tells consumers which sources to trust.

misconceptions: Learners think governance is a committee. It is owners, definitions and controls built into the platform.
Learners think a catalogue fills itself. Descriptions and owners need a person; lineage and statistics can be automatic.
Learners write policies as documents. A policy without an enforcing control is a hope.
sequence: Three people: the sales director, an analyst who defines 'active customer', and the platform engineer. Who owns, stewards and runs?
Sort metadata items into technical, business and operational.
Turn 'delete data after 24 months' into a job and a check.
Use a certification badge and see how consumers choose.
examples: Sales director: owner of the sales dataset; analyst: steward who maintains the definition of 'active customer'; platform engineer: custodian.
Technical metadata: schema and data types. Business metadata: owner, glossary term, description. Operational metadata: last refresh, row count, query frequency.
A 24-month retention policy becomes a scheduled delete of rows older than 24 months plus a check that none remain.
